plain: The claim is that Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, the Russian pioneer called the father of Russian rocketry, believed he was in touch with angelic beings and wrote about it. The religious studies scholar Diana Pasulka, author of the book American Cosmic about belief in UFOs and technology, tells Michels this herself. She says Tsiolkovsky 'believed in NHI,' meaning non-human intelligence, and 'wrote books about it.' Michels repeats it several times, sometimes crediting Pasulka and sometimes in his own words. He calls Tsiolkovsky's worldview 'cosmism' and describes it as a cosmic religion that inspired the Russian space program. In one telling, drawing on American Cosmic, Michels says Tsiolkovsky believed 'ethereal beings' were speaking to us through celestial symbols. Tsiolkovsky's 1928 pamphlet Unknown Intelligent Forces, read here in a Russian online text that may not be complete, says an influence on us by living beings 'like us, only more perfect' is very possible. It also says some facts 'speak for the intervention of some incomprehensible forces in human acts.' The text speaks of such influence in general, not of a meeting of his own, so that he himself was in touch with such beings is the tellers' step, which it neither states nor excludes. If true, the space age would have begun partly as a spiritual quest.

discussion.text: Tsiolkovsky's 1928 pamphlet Unknown Intelligent Forces, in the Russian Wikisource text read here (which may not be the whole pamphlet), says an influence on us of living beings "подобных нам, только более совершенных" (like us, only more perfect) is very possible, and that some facts "говорят за вмешательство каких-то непонятных сил в человеческие поступки" (speak for the intervention of some incomprehensible forces in human acts); beings more perfect than us who act on human affairs are what the tellers call angelic. The text read here speaks of that influence in general, not of a meeting of his own, so that he was himself in touch with such beings is the tellers' step, which it neither states nor excludes.
